lessons.title: Lesson 1: Spotting your own stress signals
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name three early signs that stress is building in you.
This lesson builds toward: After keeping a one-day stress log, you will name three of your own early stress signals in your body, thoughts, feelings or actions, with each signal written in your own words.
Stress is your body's alarm. It speeds up your heart and breathing so you can handle a challenge. A little stress can help you focus before a test, a game or a job interview. The problem is when the alarm stays on for days or weeks.
Stress shows up in four places. In your body: tight shoulders, headaches, an upset stomach, a racing heart. In your thoughts: worry that loops, trouble focusing, expecting the worst. In your feelings: short temper, sadness, feeling numb or on edge. In your actions: sleeping too much or too little, eating differently, drinking or smoking more, pulling away from people.
Everyone's signals are different. A coach may notice they snap at players. A grandmother may notice she cannot sleep. If you learn your own early signals, you can act before stress gets big.
Step by step:
- Think of the last time you felt very stressed.
- Ask: what did I feel in my body, think, feel and do?
- Write down the earliest signs you noticed.
- Pick your top three. These are your early warning lights.
Words to know:
- Stress: the body and mind's reaction to pressure or a challenge.
- Signal: a sign that tells you something is happening, like a warning light in a car.
Try it now: Keep a quick stress log for one day. Three times today (morning, afternoon, night), write: stress level from 0 to 10, and one thing you noticed in your body, thoughts, feelings or actions. Circle your top three signals.
You can now name your own early stress signals in your body, thoughts, feelings and actions.

check.q: Which is a stress signal in your body?
options: Tight shoulders or a clenched jaw
check.why: Tight muscles are a common early body signal of stress.

check.q: You notice you snap at family most evenings this week. What would you do?
options: Write it in your stress log as a possible signal
check.why: Noticing and writing down signals helps you act before stress grows.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Calming your body fast: breathing and grounding
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use slow breathing and a grounding exercise to calm down in a few minutes.
This lesson builds toward: When you feel stress building, you will use box breathing and 5-4-3-2-1 grounding to calm your body, rating your stress from 0 to 10 before and after.
When stress hits, slow breathing tells your body it is safe to turn the alarm down. One easy method is box breathing: breathe in for 4 counts, hold for 4, breathe out for 4, hold for 4. Repeat four times. If holding feels hard, just make the out-breath longer than the in-breath, for example in for 4 and out for 6.
Grounding pulls your mind back to right now when worry runs ahead. Try 5-4-3-2-1: name 5 things you see, 4 things you can touch, 3 things you hear, 2 things you smell and 1 thing you taste. You can do it anywhere: on a bus, before a meeting, in a locker room, in a waiting room.
These skills work better with practice. Try them when you are calm, so they are ready when you need them. Free phone apps can guide you, but you do not need any app. If breathing exercises make you dizzy, stop and breathe normally.
Step by step:
- Notice a stress signal.
- Box breathing: in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4. Repeat four times.
- If worry keeps running: do 5-4-3-2-1 grounding.
- Check your stress level again from 0 to 10.
Words to know:
- Box breathing: breathing in, holding, breathing out and holding, each for the same count, usually 4.
- Grounding: using your senses to bring your attention back to the present moment.
Official sources:
- National Institute of Mental Health: I'm So Stressed Out! fact sheet
Try it now: Rate your stress from 0 to 10. Do four rounds of box breathing, then one round of 5-4-3-2-1 grounding. Rate your stress again and write down both numbers.
You can now calm your body in a few minutes with slow breathing and bring your mind back with grounding.

check.q: What does 5-4-3-2-1 grounding help you do?
options: Bring your mind to the present using your senses
check.why: Grounding uses your five senses to pull your attention back to the present.

check.q: You feel your heart racing before a hard phone call. What would you do?
options: Hold your breath as long as you can
Do a few rounds of box breathing, then make the call
Cancel all calls for the week
check.why: Slow box breathing can calm your body in a few minutes.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Daily habits that protect you: sleep, movement, food and people
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick two small daily habits that make stress easier to handle.
This lesson builds toward: For the coming week, you will choose two small daily habits for sleep, movement, food or people and plan when you will do them, with a time or reminder set for each.
Breathing helps in the moment. Habits help every day. The CDC says most adults need 7 or more hours of sleep a night, and teens 13 to 17 need 8 to 10. Good sleep habits: go to bed and wake up at the same time, keep the room dark, calm and cool, put screens away about 30 minutes before bed, and limit caffeine late in the day and alcohol near bedtime.
Movement burns off stress. The CDC says adults need about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, such as 30 minutes on 5 days, plus muscle-strengthening on 2 days. A brisk walk counts. Athletes: rest days and sleep are part of training too. Regular meals and enough water also steady your mood.
People protect you. Time with someone who helps you feel better, even a short call, lowers stress. Writing in a journal and limiting news and social media when they upset you help too. Start small: one habit you can keep beats five you drop.
Step by step:
- Look at your stress log from Lesson 1.
- Pick two habits: one for sleep or movement, one for people or downtime.
- Make each one small and specific ("walk 15 minutes after lunch").
- Do them for one week and notice the difference.
Words to know:
- Habit: something you do so often that it becomes automatic.
- Moderate activity: movement that makes you breathe harder but still lets you talk, like a brisk walk.
Official sources:
- CDC: About Sleep
- CDC: Adult Activity guidelines
Try it now: Write down two small habits for this week, one for sleep or movement and one for people or downtime, with when you will do them. Set a phone reminder or write them on your calendar.
You can now choose and schedule small daily habits for sleep, movement and connection that protect you from stress.

check.q: Which habit goal is easiest to keep?
options: "Exercise two hours every day starting today"
check.why: Small, specific habits with a set time are easier to keep.

check.q: You often scroll your phone in bed until late. What small habit would you try?
options: Put the phone away about 30 minutes before bed
Use the phone more to get tired
check.why: Putting screens away before bed is a sleep tip taught in this lesson.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Getting support and helping others

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Talking to someone and asking for help
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Start a conversation to ask a person you trust for support.
This lesson builds toward: With a person you trust, you will start a conversation that says what is going on and what you need, using your own first two sentences.
Many people wait too long to talk because they feel weak, ashamed, or do not want to be a burden. Asking for help is a skill, not a weakness. Coaches, soldiers, farmers and business owners all depend on a team.
Who you can talk to: a friend or family member, a faith leader, a coach, a mentor or sponsor, a case manager or reentry counselor, a teacher or school counselor, your doctor, or a counselor or therapist. Your doctor can check for health causes and help you find mental health care. In the US, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357) is a free, confidential, 24/7 referral line for mental health and substance use; it connects you to local treatment and support groups but does not give counseling itself. Veterans can also ask their VA health team.
How to start: pick a calm time, say it simply, and say what you need. For example: "I have been really stressed lately and not sleeping. Can I talk to you for a few minutes? I mostly need you to listen." An AI chatbot can help you practice the words, but it is not a counselor. Do not type private details into it, and in a crisis, reach a real person.
Step by step:
- Choose one person you trust.
- Pick a calm time and place.
- Say what is going on in one or two sentences.
- Say what you need: listening, advice, help with a task, or help finding a professional.
Words to know:
- Counselor or therapist: a trained professional who helps people with stress, feelings and mental health.
- Referral: being pointed or sent to the right service or professional.
- Confidential: kept private.
Official sources:
- SAMHSA National Helpline
Try it now: Write the first two sentences you would say to one person you trust about your stress, including what you need from them. If you feel ready, send the message or have the talk this week.
You can now choose a person to talk to, start the conversation in plain words, and say what kind of support you need.

check.q: What is a good first sentence when asking for support?
options: "I've been really stressed lately, and I'd like to talk for a few minutes."
check.why: Saying simply what is going on and what you need opens the door to help.

check.q: You feel stressed and use an AI chatbot at night. What would you do if you start to feel unsafe?
options: Keep talking only to the chatbot
Reach a real person, such as 988 in the US or your local crisis line
Turn off your phone and wait
check.why: A chatbot can help practice words, but in a crisis you reach a real person.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Warning signs and getting crisis help
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Spot serious warning signs in yourself or someone else and know who to call.
This lesson builds toward: Given signs of crisis in yourself or someone else, you will spot the warning signs of suicide and contact the right crisis help, with crisis numbers saved in your phone and the words to ask directly ready.
Sometimes stress turns into something more serious. The National Institute of Mental Health lists warning signs of suicide, including: talking about wanting to die, feeling hopeless or trapped, feeling like a burden, looking for ways to die, giving away important things or saying goodbye, pulling away from people, more alcohol or drug use, big mood swings, and big changes in sleep or eating. Signs that are new or getting worse need help fast.
If you see signs in someone else: ask them directly and calmly, "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" Asking does not put the idea in their head. Listen without judging, stay with them, and help them connect to help. If someone is in immediate danger, call your emergency number (911 in the US).
Crisis help in the US: call or text 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org, for the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. It is free, confidential and open 24/7, with Spanish text and chat. Veterans, service members and their families: call 988 and press 1, or text 838255, for the Veterans Crisis Line; you do not need to be enrolled in VA care. Outside the US, call your country's local crisis line or emergency number; save it in your phone today.
Also get help (from your doctor or a counselor) when stress or worry does not go away, gets in the way of daily life, or makes you avoid things you need to do.
Step by step:
- Notice the warning sign.
- Ask directly and listen without judging.
- Stay with the person; do not leave them alone if they are in danger.
- Call or text 988 together (veterans: 988 then press 1), or your local crisis line.
- Immediate danger: call 911 or your emergency number.
Words to know:
- Crisis: a moment when someone's safety or ability to cope is at serious risk.
- 988 Lifeline: the US 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline: call or text 988 for free, private help any time.
Official sources:
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
- Veterans Crisis Line
- National Institute of Mental Health: Warning Signs of Suicide
Try it now: Save the crisis numbers for where you live in your phone right now: in the US, 988 (and 988 then press 1 for veterans); outside the US, your local crisis line and emergency number. Then write the exact words you would use to ask a friend if they are thinking about suicide.
You can now spot serious warning signs, ask someone directly, and connect them or yourself to crisis help.

check.q: Which of these is a warning sign of suicide?
options: Talking about being a burden or wanting to die
Being busy with a new job
check.why: Talking about being a burden or wanting to die is a serious warning sign.

check.q: A veteran friend tells you they have a plan to end their life. What would you do?
options: Stay with them and call 988 and press 1, or 911 if they are in immediate danger
check.why: Stay with them and connect them to crisis help right away.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Making your personal coping plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page plan that tells you what to do when stress builds.
This lesson builds toward: Using what you practiced in this course, you will write a one-page personal coping plan, with all six parts, saved on your phone and on paper.
When you are very stressed, it is hard to think clearly. A coping plan is a short page you write while you are calm, so you know what to do when things get hard.
Your plan has six parts: your early stress signals, your calming skills, your daily habits, people you can talk to, professional help, and crisis numbers. Keep it short and in your own words.
Keep the plan where you can reach it: on paper in your wallet or bag, and on your phone. Share it with one person you trust. Look at it again every few months, after a big change like a new job, a move, a season ending or coming home.
Step by step:
- Write your top three early stress signals.
- Write two calming skills you have practiced.
- Write two daily habits you will keep.
- Write two people you can talk to, with how to reach them.
- Write one place for professional help, and your crisis numbers.
Words to know:
- Coping plan: a short written plan of what you will do and who you will call when stress builds.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page coping plan with all six parts, including 988 (and 988 then press 1 for veterans) or your local crisis line. Save a copy on your phone and keep one on paper.
You can now write and use a personal coping plan that tells you exactly what to do and who to call when stress builds.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Early signals Fewer than three signals, or they are too general, such as "stress". Three personal early signals in the learner's own words. Signals come from a real stress log and cover body, thoughts or actions. Calming skills Calming skills listed but not practiced. Two calming skills practiced, with before-and-after stress ratings. Notes when and where each skill works best for them. Daily habits Habits are vague or have no time. Two small habits with a time or reminder for each. Habits have been tried for at least a few days. Support people and help No people listed, or no way to reach them. Two people with how to reach them, and one place to get professional help. The learner has already talked with one of them. Crisis numbers Crisis numbers are missing or wrong for where they live. 988 (and 988 then press 1 for veterans) or the local crisis line and emergency number are in the plan and saved in the phone. Also knows the words to ask a friend directly about suicide. Plan kept close The plan is missing parts or is not saved. All six parts on one page, kept on paper and on the phone. Shared with a trusted person. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which part of a coping plan comes first to help you act early?
check.why: Knowing your signals tells you when to use the rest of the plan.

check.q: Your coping plan is finished. What would you do with it?
options: Throw it away after reading it once
Keep it on paper and on your phone, and share it with someone you trust
Hide it so no one ever sees it
check.why: Keeping the plan close and shared means it is there when you need it.
